title: Arithmetic Progressions — Chapter Summary
intro: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which consecutive terms differ by a fixed constant called the common difference d. APs model anything that changes by the same step each time — salary increments, loan instalments, stacked rows, savings. Two compact formulas — the nth term aₙ = a + (n−1)d and the sum Sₙ = n/2 · [2a + (n−1)d] — answer almost every question you will face.

sections.heading: Sequences and APs
bullets: A sequence is an ordered list a₁, a₂, a₃, … .
An AP has a constant common difference d = aₙ − aₙ₋₁.
Standard form: a, a + d, a + 2d, … .
d > 0 → increasing; d < 0 → decreasing; d = 0 → constant.
To test: compute consecutive differences; all equal ⇒ AP.
An AP may be finite (last term l) or infinite.

sections.heading: The nth term
bullets: From a, d you can reach any specified term.
Reverse: given aₙ, solve a + (n−1)d = aₙ for n.
If two terms aₘ, aₙ are known, d = (aₙ − aₘ)/(n − m).
The last term of a finite AP is l = a + (n−1)d.

sections.heading: Sum of first n terms
bullets: If last term l is known, Sₙ = n/2 · (a + l).
Pairing trick: first + last = second + second-last = … = a + l.
Given Sₙ, solve quadratic in n; both positive roots may be valid.

sections.heading: Arithmetic mean
bullets: AM of a and b is (a + b)/2.
a, AM, b is a 3-term AP.
To insert n AMs between a and b: d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
kth AM: A_k = a + k · d, k = 1, 2, …, n.

sections.heading: Applications
bullets: Equal-step real-world quantities are APs.
Loan instalments, salary with fixed increment, stacked rows.
Production / savings schedules with constant increments.
Identify a, d, n; then apply aₙ or Sₙ as appropriate.

key_takeaways: Test for AP by computing all consecutive differences; they must be equal.
Memorise aₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2 · [2a + (n − 1)d] — every problem reduces to these.
If you know two terms, recover d via (aₙ − aₘ)/(n − m).
When the last term l is known, Sₙ = n/2 · (a + l) is faster.
Inserting n AMs splits the gap (b − a) into (n + 1) equal parts.
Many word problems are APs in disguise — read for 'fixed increment' or 'fixed reduction'.

glossary.definition: An ordered list of numbers a₁, a₂, a₃, … indexed by their position.
One member of a sequence; the nth term is aₙ.
A sequence whose consecutive terms differ by the same constant; written a, a+d, a+2d, … .
The starting term of the AP, also denoted a₁.
The fixed constant d = aₙ − aₙ₋₁ shared by every consecutive pair.
The final term of a finite AP; equals a + (n − 1)d for an n-term AP.
An AP with d > 0; each term exceeds the previous one.
An AP with d < 0; each term is smaller than the previous one.
An AP with d = 0; every term equals the first term a.
aₙ = a + (n − 1) · d — gives any term directly from a and d.
Sₙ = n/2 · [2a + (n − 1) · d]; equivalently Sₙ = n/2 · (a + l) when the last term l is known.
The single-number average (a + b)/2; placing it between a and b creates a 3-term AP.
Building an (n + 2)-term AP a, A₁, …, Aₙ, b with common difference d = (b − a)/(n + 1).
An AP with a fixed number of terms and a last term l.
An AP that continues without a last term; only aₙ has a value at every index n.
